AN IDENTIFIER WRITTEN FROM INFERENCE READS EXACTLY LIKE ONE THAT WAS MEASURED, AND A COMMIT MESSAGE IS THE WORST PLACE TO PUT ONE. 5ef7c75's message names 15e4a3d as the commit carrying cc's event files. They are in 4bdf371, established with `git log --diff-filter=A` -- the one command that answers it, run only after vc pushed back. The sha was assembled from a peer saying it had committed boards, the files having become tracked, and one commit having "wb" in its subject. A wrong sha in prose is a nuisance; in a durable record it sends the next reader somewhere real and wrong.

A COMMENT CAN DISARM THE CHECKER AND THE CHECKER STILL EXITS 0. shellcheck reads `# shellcheck ` as DIRECTIVE syntax, so a sentence that opens that way is a parse error (SC1072/SC1073) and it answers by SKIPPING the rest of that script's checks. Found by vc in Intent's tests.yml, where the sentence began `# shellcheck IS AN ARMED TOOL FOR THIS PROJECT` -- silent since it was written, in the one project that arms shellcheck as a critic. Devbin's own tree is clean of it, which I checked rather than assumed on 2026-09-22: every `# shellcheck` line here carries one of the six real directive keys. The general shape is the one to carry: a tool whose OWN configuration surface accepts prose will take a comment as configuration, and disarming is not a failure it reports.

AN INSTRUMENT POINTED AT THE WRONG THING ANSWERS CLEANLY RATHER THAN ERRORING, AND IT HAPPENED TWICE IN ONE DAY. Re-checking which commit carried cc's event files, a grep for the node name on one line returned ZERO in both candidate commits -- the shape puts subject.type and subject.id on separate lines, so it could never match, and the clean zero agreed with neither the old claim nor the true one. Then `git rev-list <remote-tracking>..HEAD` read 23 unpushed in a repo whose HEAD was already on a pushed branch, and read a missing origin/main as NOT BACKED UP in four repos whose remote was simply named something else -- one keystroke from reporting a data-loss emergency that was three real repos and two false ones. `jq` over the structure and `git ls-remote` against the live remote are what answer those two questions. A tracking ref is a cached opinion, not the remote. Ask what the instrument is actually reading before you read its zero or its silence.

AN INSTRUMENT POINTED AT THE WRONG THING ANSWERS CLEANLY RATHER THAN ERRORING. Three instances on 2026-09-22, all returning a clean number that was not an error: (1) a one-line grep for a node name returned ZERO cc event files in BOTH candidate commits, because the event shape puts subject.type and subject.id on separate lines -- it agreed with neither the old claim nor the truth; jq over the structure answered it. (2) git rev-list <remote-tracking>..HEAD read 23 unpushed in a repo whose HEAD was on a pushed branch, and read four repos as NOT BACKED UP whose remote was simply named something other than origin -- one keystroke from reporting a data-loss emergency that was three real repos and two false ones; git ls-remote against the live remote answered it. (3) jq over intent wb show <node> --json with select(.kind=="todo") returned 34 todos where the board prints 10, because a generated board carries ARCHIVED rows beside live ones and there is a state field -- select(.kind=="todo" and .state=="live") is the query. What caught (3) was the count disagreeing with the rendered board, which is why a list and a count that disagree is a caught error and a list alone is a silent one. A tracking ref is a cached opinion, not the remote; a JSON view is the whole store, not the rendering. Ask what the instrument is actually reading before you trust its zero, its silence, or its clean total.

A CHECK THAT ANSWERS CLEANLY HAS NOT NECESSARILY MEASURED WHAT YOU ASKED, AND THE CLEAN ANSWER CARRIES NO SIGN OF IT. Four instances to 2026-09-22, not one of which errored. (1) BSD `cmp -n <bytes of the shorter file>` reaches EOF and exits 1 though every compared byte matched, reporting two appended issue bodies as CHANGED; its control used a shorter limit and never reached EOF, so the control had the right polarity and the wrong SHAPE -- `diff` was the evidence. (2) shellcheck parses `# shellcheck ` as DIRECTIVE syntax, so a sentence opening that way is SC1072/SC1073 and it SKIPS the rest of that script's checks -- found by vc in Intent's tests.yml, silent since it was written, in the one project that arms shellcheck as a critic; devbin's own tree was checked clean on 2026-09-22 rather than assumed. (3) Three wrong populations in one day: a grep for a node name returned ZERO cc event files in both candidate commits because `subject.type` and `subject.id` sit on separate lines; `git rev-list <remote-tracking>..HEAD` read 23 unpushed in a repo whose HEAD was on a pushed branch, and four repos as NOT BACKED UP whose remote was simply not named `origin`, one keystroke from a false data-loss emergency; `jq ... select(.kind=="todo")` returned 34 where the board prints 10, because a generated board carries archived rows beside live ones -- `select(.kind=="todo" and .state=="live")` is the query. (4) vc's own, 2026-09-22: a command's exit status measured through a pipe read `tail`'s status rather than the command's, giving rc=0 for a command that exits 3. Re-reading that number could never have found it; only re-taking the measurement bare did. THE TELL IS NEVER IN THE ANSWER. A tracking ref is a cached opinion, not the remote; a JSON view is the whole store, not the rendering; a pipeline's status belongs to its LAST stage; and a linter that skipped your file exits 0 exactly like one that passed it. Ask what the instrument actually read before trusting its zero, its silence or its clean total -- and when a count and a rendering disagree, that disagreement is the only free error detection on offer.
